rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham continues the tender appeal, asking his father to follow him so he can guide him to clear truth; he presents the invitation gently because his father lacks divine knowledge and sound independent judgment.
rows.anchor: ثم دعاه إلى أن يتبعه ليهديه إلى الحق المبين لما أنه لم يكن محظوظا من العلم الالهى مستقلا بالنظر السوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He avoids calling his father extremely ignorant or himself exceptionally learned, instead presenting himself as a gentle son who better knows the path they are taking.
rows.anchor: ولم يسم أباه بالجهل المفرط وإن كان في اقصاه ولا نفسه بالعلم الفائق وإن كان كذلك بل ابرز نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound, upright path reaches the highest aims and turns away from error that leads to ruin.
rows.anchor: أي مستقيما موصلا إلى أسنى المطالب منحنيا عن الضلال المؤدي إلى مهاوى الردى والمعاطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording “came to me” apparently places this conversation after Abraham had been made a prophet.
rows.anchor: هذه المحاورة كانت بعد أن نبئ عليه السلام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies the knowledge as complete knowledge of what is necessary, impossible, and possible for God.
rows.anchor: والذي جاءه قيل العلم بما يجب لله تعالى وما يمتنع في حقه وما يجوز على اتم وجه واكمله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the knowledge as knowledge of afterlife matters, reward, and punishment.
rows.anchor: العلم بأمور الآخرة وثوابها وعقابها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A third interpretation says Abraham received knowledge encompassing both the divine matters and the afterlife.
rows.anchor: العلم بما يعم ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worshipping idols is worship of Satan because Satan prompts people toward idols and entices them to worship them.
rows.anchor: فان عبادتك الأصنام عبادة له إذ هو الذي يسولها ويغريك عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Satan disobedient to the All-Merciful explains and reinforces the prohibition: one who obeys a rebel is himself disobedient, and rebels merit loss of favor and punishment.
rows.anchor: تعليل لموجب النهي وتأكيد له ببيان أنه مستعص على من شملتك رحمته وعمتك نعمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming the Lord as al-Rahman highlights the severity of Satan's rebellion, while mentioning only disobedience points to its foundational role in his other sins or his hostility to Adam.
rows.anchor: وللاشارة إلى هذا المعنى جئ بالرحمن وفيه أيضا إشارة إلى كمال شناعة عصيانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recalling Satan's disobedience to God should prompt Abraham's father to avoid Satan's allegiance and obedience; the explicit name in place of a pronoun adds emphasis.
rows.anchor: فتذكيره داع لأبيه عن الأحتراز عن موالاته وطاعته والأظهار في موضع الاضمار لزيادة التقرير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement warns of the bad end of idol worship; fear means expecting harm on the basis of a probable or certain sign, so it does not assert certainty.
rows.anchor: تحذير من سوء عاقبة ما هو فيه من عبادة الأصنام والخوف كما قال الراغب توقع المكروه عن أمارة مظنونه أو معلومة

rows.speaker: الفراء والطبري
rows.claim: Al-Farra and al-Tabari construe “I fear” as “I know”; al-Alusi says this interpretation is not apt.
rows.anchor: وحملة الفراء والطبري على العلم وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: السعد
rows.claim: Al-Saʿd says the indefinite “punishment” can suggest either magnification, a terrible punishment, or minimization, even the slightest punishment.
rows.anchor: التعظيم والتقليل أي عذاب هائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “touch” and the attribution of punishment to al-Rahman do not prove that the punishment is slight; punishment from a generous, forbearing Lord can be especially severe.
rows.anchor: وقال لا دلالة للفظ المس وإضافة العذاب إلى الرحمن على ترجيح الثاني كما ذكره بعضهم

rows.speaker: أبو السعود
rows.claim: Abu al-Suʿud prefers magnification: “from” modifies an implied description, adding relational grandeur to the inherent grandeur of the indefinite noun; al-Rahman signals that mercy does not prevent punishment.
rows.anchor: واختار اب السعود أنه للتعظيم

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf objects that magnification conflicts with the context of compassion and courtesy; the warning's “from al-Rahman” recalls 19:44 and presents punishment as mercy and a reminder that mercy precedes wrath.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف أن الحمل على التفخيم في عذاب كما جوزه صاحب المفتاح مما يأباه المقام أي لأنه مقام اظهار مزيد الشفقة

rows.speaker: القونوي
rows.claim: Al-Qunawi explains that al-Rahman combines gentleness and severity for people facing majesty, whereas al-Rahim is associated with people of the right and beauty.
rows.anchor: فقد قال المحقق القونوي في تفسير الفاتحة الرحيم كما بينا لأهل اليمين والجمال والرحمن الجامع بين اللطف والقهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi favors magnification because it better serves the warning, while allowing that a severe tone can itself arise from compassion.
rows.anchor: وكاني بك تختار التفخيم لأنه أنسب بالتخويف وتدعى أنه ههنا من معدن الشفقة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported poetic maxim says that one may sometimes be harsh with someone one pities so that the person takes warning; courtesy also lies in not asserting that punishment will certainly strike.
rows.anchor: فقسا ليزدجروا ومن يك حازما فليقس احيانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The magnitude of the punishment may be measured by its consequences rather than by the initial touch itself, allowing the word to suggest either magnitude or smallness in different respects.
rows.anchor: إن الكثرة والعظمة باعتبار ما يلزمه ويتبعه لا بالنظر اليه في نفسه فانه غير مقصود بالذات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative reads the result clause as following even a slight punishment and understands “ally” as one who follows and befriends Satan, remaining under God's anger.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون فتكون الخ مترتبا على مس العذاب القليل والولي من الموالاة وهي المتابعة والمصادقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense is afterlife punishment; interpreting it as worldly abandonment or another worldly affliction is not persuasive.
rows.anchor: ثم الظاهر أن المراد بالعذاب عذاب الآخره وتأوله بعضهم بعذاب الدنيا واراد به الخذلان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some propose reversing the order: Abraham fears his father will become Satan's ally in this world and then suffer punishment in the next; al-Alusi says the apparent syntax needs no rearrangement.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن في الكلام تقديما وتاخير والأصل إني اخاف أن تكون وليا للشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father's reply is introduced as an answer to an implied question and shows him persisting in defiance, meeting Abraham's gentle advice with harshness.
rows.anchor: استئناف مبنى على سؤال نشأ من صدر الكلام كأنه قيل فماذا قال ابوه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses “rاغب” as a fronted predicate and “you” as subject; fronting directs the rebuke at the very fact of turning away and adds astonishment.
rows.anchor: مبتدأ وفيه توجيه الأنكار إلى نفس الرغبه مع ضرب من التعجيب

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء وابن مالك
rows.claim: Abu al-Baqa, Ibn Malik, and others parse “you” as the subject of the participle, licensed by the preceding interrogative, avoiding separation of “rاغب” from its complement.
rows.anchor: فاعل الصفة لتقدم الاستفهام وهو مغن عن الخبر

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf answers that the subject is not wholly foreign, since the separated phrase is a prepositional phrase understood later; the word order is rhetorically viable and heightens denial.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب الكشف : المبتدأ ليس اجنبيا من كل وجه

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers the Abu al-Baqa analysis because it avoids separation and an unusual fronting; the author also reports the rival rhetorical case for fronting as stronger in denunciation.
rows.anchor: ورجح أو حيان اعراب أبى البقاء ومن معه

rows.speaker: البدر الدماميني
rows.claim: Al-Badr al-Damamini hesitates to treat the delayed noun as subject in patterns like “Is the sun rising?”, fearing confusion with an object/agent construction.
rows.anchor: وتوقف البدر الدماميني في جواز ابتدائية المؤخر في مثل هذا التركيب وان خلا عن فصل أو محذور آخر

rows.speaker: الشمني
rows.claim: Al-Shumni replies that the first construction has two possible readings, both marked, creating ambiguity rather than the role confusion found in “Zayd struck.”
rows.anchor: واجاب الشمنى بأن زيدا في الأول يحتمل أمرين كل منهما بخلاف الأصل وذلك اجمال لا لبس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat means that if Abraham does not stop rebuking idolatry and calling his father to his message, his father will stone him.
rows.anchor: أي والله لئن لم تنته عما انت عليه من النهي عن عبادتها والدعوة إلى ما دعوتني اليه لأرجمنك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets the threatened stoning literally as throwing stones.
rows.anchor: لأرجمنك بالحجارة على ما روى عن الحسن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والسدي والضحاك وابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jurayj report a figurative threat to revile or insult Abraham with the tongue.
rows.anchor: باللسان والمراد لاشتمنك وروى ذلك عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A few construe the command as telling Abraham to stop turning away from the idols, but al-Alusi says that interpretation is not sound.
rows.anchor: وقدر بعضهم متعلق النهي الرغبه عن الآلهه أي لئن لم تنته عن الرغبه عن آلهتي لأرجمنك وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari supplies an omitted command, “beware me,” before “leave me,” avoiding a mismatch between the threat and an imperative clause.
rows.anchor: أي فاحذرني واتركني والى ذلك ذهب الزمخشري

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Others coordinate “leave me” with the preceding sentence, invoking Sibawayh's allowance for coordination between clauses of different kinds; the author notes that this ordering is more affecting.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من عطف على الجملة السابقة بناء على تجويز سيبويه العطف مع التخالف في الأخبار والإنشاء

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group interpret “for a long while” as a long duration.
rows.anchor: أي دهرا طويلا عن الحسن ومجاهد وجماعه

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi glosses the command as “begin” or “go ahead,” which al-Alusi regards as the likely contextual sense; the underlying word is linked to extension over time.
rows.anchor: السدى : ابدأ وكأنه المراد واصله على ما قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form is used adverbially for a long time, as in the line of Muhalhil describing mountains splitting and widows mourning for a long while.
rows.anchor: فتصدعت صمم الجبال لموته وبكت عليه المرملات مليا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn Abbas glosses the word as “long,” without naming the thing whose duration is meant, allowing a source or adverbial analysis.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن الأنباري عن ابن عباس أنه فسره بطويلا ولم يذكر الموصوف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas reads it as safe, sound, and able to leave before being beaten into helplessness; on this reading it describes Abraham's condition.
rows.anchor: وفي روايه أخرى عن ابن عباس أن المعنى سالما سويا والمراد قادرا على الهجر مطيقا له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Peace be upon you” is a farewell and a way of answering evil with good: Abraham promises neither to harm nor address his father hurtfully.
rows.anchor: توديع ومتاركة على طريقة مقابلة السيئة بالحسنة فان ترك الأساءة للمسيء إحسان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the words as a greeting of farewell and allows initiating the prescribed greeting to an unbeliever, as Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna held.
rows.anchor: تحية مفارق وجوز قائل هذا تحية الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects the evidence for greeting unbelievers with salām: its proof-texts are interpreted away, and Sahih Muslim forbids initiating greeting to Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: وما استدل به متأول وهو محجوج بما ثبت في صحيح مسلم لا تبدءوا اليهود والنصارى بالسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word is read nominative as a noun or accusative as an absolute verbal noun.
rows.anchor: بالنصب على المصدرية والرفع على الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's promised forgiveness means asking God to guide his father to faith and enable repentance, as his other prayer explains.
rows.anchor: أي استدعيه سبحانه أن يغفر لك بأن يوفقك للتوبه ويهديك إلى الأيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking guidance for a living unbeliever whose final fate is unknown is permitted; requesting it after God has revealed that the person will die in unbelief is impossible and prohibited.
rows.anchor: مما لاريب فيه جوازه كما أنه لاريب في عدم جوازه

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi explains that believers were told these hostile unbelievers are God's enemies, urged to sever kinship, and then directed to Abraham as a model of estrangement, with his compassionate promise excepted because their unbelief was not yet known.
rows.anchor: ثم بالغ جل شأنه في تفصيل عدواتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The objection is that believers' prohibited prayer for unbelieving relatives, often identified as the Prophet's prayer for Abu Talib, cannot have meant asking for guidance after death—or after his unbelief was established in life.
rows.anchor: أن الأستغفار الذي وقع من المؤمنين لأولى قرابتهم فنهوا عنه لأنه كان بعد التبين كان كاستغفار إبراهيم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Abraham's prayer could have been conditioned on repentance and faith, and cites the report that his father promised to believe; another reading has “his father” rather than “to him.”
rows.anchor: اراد اشتراط التوبة عن الكفر وقالوا آمنا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari also argues that only revelation prohibited forgiveness for unbelievers; reason alone did not, so Abraham's promise and fulfillment could have preceded the prohibition.
rows.anchor: الذي منع من الأستغفار للكافر انما هو السميع فاما قضية العقل فلا تأباه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He argues that the exception of Abraham's promise from the command to imitate him would be pointless if the promise were merely conditional on the father's faith.
rows.anchor: أنه استثنى قول إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf records al-Razi's objection that the exception only removes the duty to imitate Abraham, not the permissibility of the act; it answers that al-Zamakhshari treats the act as not sinful for Abraham, only prohibited for later believers by revelation.
rows.anchor: واعترض الأمام حديث الأستثناء بأن الآية دلت على المنع من التأسى لا أن ذلك كان معصية

rows.speaker: صاحب التقريب
rows.claim: The author of al-Taqrib objects that exclusion from what must be imitated proves the act is not obligatory, not that it is impermissible; he says the verse does not establish a duty to imitate.
rows.anchor: واعترض صاحب التقريب بأن نفي اللازم ممنوع فان الأستثناء عما وجبت فيه الأسوة دل على أنه غير واجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi replies that the act is called objectionable and excluded from the good example, so copying it would turn that example into a bad one; the obligation to follow the model is stated elsewhere.
rows.anchor: والجواب أن جعله مستنكرا ومستثنى يدل على أنه منكر لا الأستثناء عما وجبت فيه فقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's action was not inherently wrong, but later revelation made such prayer forbidden; whether it had been permitted before the prohibition by reason or by revelation is disputed.
rows.anchor: والحاصل أن فعل إبراهيم عليه السلام يدل على أنه ليس منكرا في نفسه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say pre-prohibition permission followed reason; others, identified as the Sunni view, ground it in revelation because it falls under kindness to parents and compassion for those invited to faith, while the first is attributed to the Muʿtazila.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الزمخشري جعل مدرك الجواز قبل النهي العقل وهي مسئلة خلافية وكم قائل أنه السمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says that if Abraham's prayer became forbidden after revelation, the Prophet would not have prayed for Abu Talib; the reply is that he may not yet have received the prohibition.
rows.anchor: واعترض القول بأنه استنكر في زمن إبراهيم عليه السلام بعد ما كان غير منكر بأنه لو كان كذلك لم يفعله نبينا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking faith for a living unbeliever of unknown destiny is permitted by reason and revelation, but not for one known to be sealed against faith; asking forgiveness while one remains an unbeliever is likewise unsound.
rows.anchor: أن الأستغفار للكافر الحي المجهول العاقبة بمعنى طلب هدايته للايمان مما لا محذور فيه عقلا ونقلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reason against requesting forgiveness while unbelief continues is that it would trivialize unbelief and make the supreme obligation of faith pointless; the reasoning may extend to other sins, unless unbelief is distinguished.
rows.anchor: وصيرورة التكليف بالأيمان الذي لا شئ يعدله من الطاعات عبثا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reason alone does not forbid requesting forgiveness for an unbeliever already dead in unbelief; revelation does, because the prior rationale for a living person's continuing unbelief does not apply.
rows.anchor: وأما طلب المغفرة للكافر بعد موته على الكفر فلا تأباه قضية العقل وإنما يمنعه السمع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reconciliation says the Prophet continued praying for Abu Talib until 9:113 descended, reading “after it became clear” as after their death in unbelief and placing 4:48 later.
rows.anchor: لا ازال أستغفر لك مالم أنه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reconciliation needs no chronology: out of compassion the Prophet understood that God would not forgive shirk without intercession or involving every limb, believed Abu Talib's shirk was not of that kind, and prayed until forbidden.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا حاجة إلى التزام ذلك لجواز أن يكون عليه الصلاة والسلام لو فور شفقة وشدة رافته قد حمل الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kind to me” means abundantly gracious and attentive to honoring Abraham; this explains the preceding promise.
rows.anchor: بليغا في البر والأكرام يقال حفى به اذا اعتنى باكرامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause explains the preceding statement, with the adverb moved forward for the verse's cadence and emphasis.
rows.anchor: والجملة تعليل المضمون ماقبلها وتقديم الظرف لرعاية الفواصل مع الأهتمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I will leave you” apparently coordinates with “I will seek forgiveness”: Abraham will separate from his father and people by migrating because his counsel had no effect.
rows.anchor: والمراد اتباعد عنك وعن قومك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Reports say Abraham migrated to Syria, or to nearby Harran, while his people were in Kutha.
rows.anchor: وقيل إلى حران وهو قريب من ذلك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A spiritual interpretation takes the separation as inward separation in heart and belief, but al-Alusi calls this contrary to the apparent and transmitted sense.
rows.anchor: وجوز حمل على العتزال بالقلب والاعتقاد وهو خلاف الظاهر المأثور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling on God means worshipping Him alone; “worship” answers the father's complaint about abandoning idols, while “call” more clearly expresses the positive turn toward God.
rows.anchor: أي اعبده سبحانه وحده كما يفهم من اجتناب غيره تعالى من المعبودات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The call may mean supplication generally, or Abraham's prayers for wisdom and the company of the righteous, or for a righteous child.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يراد بذلك الدعاء مطلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Wretched” means disappointed and unsuccessful; the wording indirectly contrasts Abraham's hope with his people's misery in worshipping idols.
rows.anchor: خائبا ضائع السعى وفيه تعريض بشقاوتهم في عبادة الهتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beginning with “perhaps” shows humility and proper etiquette, since acceptance is God's favor rather than an obligation and the final outcome is among the unseen matters known to God.
rows.anchor: وفي تصدير الكلام بعسى من اظهار التواضع ومراعاة حسن الأدب والتنبيه على حقيقة الحق من أن الاثابه والأجابة بطريق التفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Abraham migrated away from his father and people, God gave him Isaac and Jacob in place of the family he left, though the births did not immediately follow the migration.
rows.anchor: بدل بن فارقهم من أبيه وقومه الكفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The better-known chronology has Ishmael first, after Abraham's prayer for a righteous child; Hagar came, Sarah became jealous, then Isaac was born and later Jacob.
rows.anchor: والمشهور أن أول ما وهب له عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order of the gift highlights how great God's compensation was for leaving kin: Isaac and Jacob became ancestors of many eminent prophets and descendants; Ishmael is then singled out for his own merit.
rows.anchor: ولعل ترتيب هبتهما على اعتزاله ههنا لبيان كمال عظم النعم التى اعطاها الله تعالى اياه بمقابله من اعتزالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nearer account says Abraham first went to Harran, married Sarah, and had Isaac, from whom Jacob was born.
rows.anchor: وروى أنه عليه السلام لما قصد الشام اتى اولا حران وتزوج سارة وولدت له إسحاق وولد لاسحق يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Each” can mean Isaac and Jacob, the two of them together, or the pair plus Abraham; the first is most natural, and the fronted object restricts the claim to each one rather than only some.
rows.anchor: أي كل واحد من إسحاق ويعقوب أو منهما

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the mercy bestowed on Abraham and his descendants was prophethood; mentioning mercy after prophethood marks it as a special divine grace.
rows.anchor: النبوة + ولعل ذكر ذلك بعد ذكر جعلهم انبياء

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi interprets the gift of mercy as wealth and children; another reported interpretation is scripture.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبى : هي المالى والولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers a comprehensive sense covering every religious and worldly good they received, beyond what anyone else received.
rows.anchor: والأظهر انعا عامة لكل خير ديني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A “lofty good mention” means people take pride in them and praise them, fulfilling Abraham's prayer for a good mention among later generations.
rows.anchor: تفتخر بهم الناس ويثنون عليهم استجابة لدعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tongue” stands for speech by cause, and can mean a language or a distinguished message; two poetic uses support the latter sense.
rows.anchor: والمراد باللسان ما يوجد به من الكلام فهو مجاز بعلاقة السببية كاليد في العطية ولسان العرب لغتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling their reputation truthful and lofty says they deserve the praise and that their virtues remain famous across ages, states, religions, and sects; a restricted interpretation is the prayer formula for Abraham, but generality is better.
rows.anchor: وخص بعضهم لسان الصدق بما يتلى في التشهد كما صليت على إبراهيم وعلى آل إبراهيم والعموم أولى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Moses may be mentioned before Ishmael to keep him next to Jacob, or to appeal quickly to the People of the Book after the appeal to Arabs.
rows.anchor: قدم ذكره على إسماعيل عليهما السلام لئلا ينفصل عن ذكر يعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sincere” may mean that Moses worshipped without shirk or ostentation, or that he surrendered himself to God and devoted himself exclusively to Him.
rows.anchor: موحدا اخلص عبادته عن الشرك والرياء أو اسلم وجهه لله عز وجل واخلص عن سواه

rows.speaker: الكوفيون وأبو رزين ويحيى وقتادة
rows.claim: The Kufans, Abu Razin, Yahya, and Qatada read the word with an open lām, meaning that God purified or chose Moses.
rows.anchor: بفتح اللام على أن الله تعالى اخلصه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was a messenger sent by God to convey the rulings He willed; “prophet” may mean elevated in rank above many messengers or above the people addressed.
rows.anchor: جهة الله تعالى إلى الخلق بتبليغ ما شاء من الأحكام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Prophet” can derive from elevation or from conveying news from God; al-Alusi prefers elevation as the stronger sense.
rows.anchor: من النبوه بمعنى الرفعه ويجوز أن يكون من النبأ

rows.speaker: الجوهري
rows.claim: Al-Jawhari says the man who addressed the Prophet with the hamza intended a slur that his people had cast him out; the Prophet's reply denied that implication while distinguishing the prophetic title.
rows.anchor: والذي ذكره الجوهري أن القائل اراد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view gives both “messenger” and “prophet” their lexical senses and explains the second term because not every envoy is a prophet; someone may be sent with a gift or letter.
rows.anchor: واختار بعضهم أن المراد من كلا اللفظين معناهما اللغوي وان ذكر النبى بعد الرسول لما أنه ليس كل مرسل نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Mount is between Egypt and Midian; its “right side” is the side on Moses' right, since a mountain itself has no right or left side.
rows.anchor: الطور جبل بين مصر ومدين والايمن صفه لجانب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Right” may instead mean blessed and qualify the side or the mountain, but the ordinary right-as-opposite-of-left reading is preferable.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الايمن من اليمين وهو البركة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent account is that Moses heard verbal speech emerging from that direction; some instead say he heard speech without letters or sound, with all his body and from every direction.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه عليه السلام انما سمع الكلام اللفظي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A mystical interpretation takes the call as Moses turning toward the blessed Mount beyond the limits of rational intellect; al-Alusi says reports point otherwise.
rows.anchor: ناديناه مقبلا من جانب الطور المبارك وهو طور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bringing Moses near as an intimate is an honor: he is likened to one whom a king draws close for private speech, choosing him as companion and removing intermediaries.
rows.anchor: تقريب تشريف مثل حاله عليه السلام بحال من قربه الملك لمناجاته واصطفاه لمصاحبته ورفع الوسائط بينه وبينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Intimate” is an active-participial sense of private conversation, used as a circumstantial accusative of Moses; another parse derives it from elevation.
rows.anchor: فعيل بمعنا مفاعل كجليس بمعنى مخالس ونديم

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: A report from Saʿid ibn Jubayr says Gabriel carried Moses behind him until Moses heard the pen's scratching and the Torah being written anew; another account says it had been written before Adam by forty years.
rows.anchor: فقد أخرج سعيد بن منصور وابن منذر ابن أبى حاتم عن سعيد بن جبير أن جبرائيل عليه السلام اردفه حتى سمع صرير القلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas, authenticated by al-Hakim, says Moses was raised to heaven until he heard the pen; this means some ascent is not exclusive to Muhammad, though his was the fullest.
rows.anchor: وخبر رفعه عليه السلام إلى السماء حتى سمع صرير القلم رواه غير واحد وصححه الحكم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains “intimate” as “saved” through Moses' truthfulness; al-Alusi considers this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: ناجيا بصدقه وروى ذلك عن قتادة ولا يخفى بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave Moses his brother Aaron as a helper and supporter, in answer to Moses' prayer for a minister from his family; Aaron himself was not the gift because he was older and already existed.
rows.anchor: أي معاضدة اخيه وموازرته اجابة لدعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grammatical reading treats “his brother” as the direct object, “Aaron” as apposition, and “prophet” as a circumstantial description.
rows.anchor: حال منه ويجوز أن تكون من للتبعيض

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take “from Our mercy” as partitive and parse “his brother” as an apposition to part or whole, or as an inclusive apposition.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون من للتبعيض قيل وحينئذ يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed partitive analyses are grammatically strained, including the suggestion that “his brother” replaces an implied “thing”; the direct-object reading is apparent.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بانها أن كانت اسما مرادفة لبعض فهو خلاف الظاهر وان كانت حرفا فابدال الأسم من الحرف

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority, rightly in al-Alusi's view, identify Ishmael as Abraham's son; the separate mention highlights special concern for him.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه ابن إبراهيم عليهما السلام كما ذهب اليه الجمهور وهو الحق وفصل ذكره عن ذكر أبيه

rows.speaker: الإمامية عن أبي عبد الله
rows.claim: An Imami report from Abu Abd Allah identifies him as Ishmael son of Ezekiel, sent to a people who scalped him; he asked God to spare them and leave their judgment to God, but al-Alusi doubts the attribution's reliability.
rows.anchor: أنه اسماعيل بن حزقيل بعثه الله تعالى إلى قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His reputation for keeping promises explains the command to remember him and was widely known.
rows.anchor: تعليل لموجب الأمر وايراده عليه السلام بهذا الوصف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A report says Ishmael waited a year for a man who asked him to stay in a place; variants give twelve days, three days, or one day and night, while the year is most famous.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء في بعض الأخبار أنه وعد رجلا أن يقيم له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Ishmael was the intended sacrifice, his promise to endure the sacrifice and fulfillment of it exemplify truthfulness; one scholar says this may be the specific promise meant.
rows.anchor: واذا كان هو الذبيح فناهيك في صدقه أنه وعد اباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling him both messenger and prophet shows that a messenger need not bring an independent law or scripture, despite stricter definitions some scholars proposed.
rows.anchor: أن فيه دلالة على أن الرسول لا يجب أن يكون صاحب شريعة مستقلة فان اولاد إبراهيم عليهم السلام كانوا على شريعته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some say a messenger must have a law only relative to his addressees; Ishmael brought Abraham's law to Jurhum, who were not themselves addressed by Abraham, but al-Alusi finds this argument weak.
rows.anchor: المراد بكونه صاحب شريعة أن يكون له شريعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ismael attended to his household's prayer and almsgiving after perfecting himself, beginning with his closest relations; alternatively, he completed the wider community through family members who served as examples.
rows.anchor: اشتغالا بالاهم وهو أن يبدأ الرجل بعد تطميل نفسه بتكميل من هو اقرب الناس اليه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets “his household” as his community, since a prophet is like a father to his community; Abdullah's codex reading “his people” supports this.
rows.anchor: المراد باهله امته لكون النبى بمنزله الأب لامته

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Prayer and zakah may have their usual meanings; alternatively zakah means general charity or purification of the soul, and a report says Ishmael enjoined prayer at night and charity by day.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالصلاة والزكاة قيل معناها المشهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He was pleasing to his Lord because his words and deeds were upright.
rows.anchor: لاستقامه اقواله وافعاله وهو اسم مفعول واصله مرضوو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive participle is morphologically derived from marduw, with its final wāw changed and assimilated; Ibn Abi Abla read the unaltered form, and Arabic also has “earth watered by buckets” in altered and unaltered forms.
rows.anchor: من غير اعلال وعن العرب أنهم قالوا : ارض منسية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Idris was a prophet before Noah, with a thousand years between them according to a report in al-Mustadrak from Ibn Abbas; he was Enoch, son of Jared, in a genealogy back to Adam.
rows.anchor: هو نبى قبل نوح وبينهما على ما في المستدرك عن ابن عباس الف سنة وهو اخنوخ بن يرد

rows.speaker: وهب بن منبه
rows.claim: Wahb ibn Munabbih calls Idris Noah's ancestor; the more common account makes him Noah's great-grandfather through Methuselah.
rows.anchor: وعن وهب بن منبه أنه جد نوح عليه السلام والمشهور أنه جد أبيه فانه ابن لمك من متوشلخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historical accounts say Idris first studied stars and calculation, wrote with a pen, sewed and wore clothing, sent thirty scrolls, established weights and measures and weapons, and fought Cain's descendants; the first achievement is attributed to al-Bahr as a miracle.
rows.anchor: وهو أول من نظر في النجوم والحساب وجعل الله تعالى ذلك من معجزاته على ما في البحر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud identifies Idris with Elijah, sent to tell his people to affirm God alone and do as they wished; they refused and were destroyed.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود أنه الياس بعث إلى قومه أن يقولوا لا اله إلا الله ويعملوا ما شاؤا فابوا واهلكوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the first identification, although Ibn Abi Hatim transmits the Elijah view from Ibn Masʿud with a sound chain.
rows.anchor: والمعول عليه الأول وان روى القول بأنه الياس ابن أبي حاتم بسند حسن عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most say “Idris” is Syriac, not derived from Arabic study; Arabic derivation is blocked by its declension, though the Syriac meaning may be similar and may allude to his extensive study.
rows.anchor: وهذا اللفظ سرياني عند الأكثرين وليس مشتقا من الدرس لأن الاشتقاق من غير العربي مما لم يقل به أحد

rows.speaker: الحسن والجبائي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, al-Jubba'i, and Abu Muslim interpret the high place as the honor of prophethood and nearness to God.
rows.anchor: هو شرف النبوة والزلفى عند الله تعالى كما روى عن الحسن واليه ذهب الجبائي وابو مسلم

rows.speaker: أنس وأبو سعيد الخدري وكعب ومجاهد
rows.claim: Anas, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, Kaʿb, and Mujahid identify the place as the fourth heaven.
rows.anchor: وعن انس وابي سعيد الخدري وكعب ومجاهد السماء الرابعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak say it is the sixth heaven.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس والضحاك السماء السادسة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another report from al-Hasan places Idris in Paradise, the highest place.
rows.anchor: وفي روايه أخر عن الحسن الجنه لا شئ اعلا من الجنه

rows.speaker: النابغة الجعدي
rows.claim: The poet al-Nabigha al-Jaʿdi said his people's fame reaches heaven and hoped for a station beyond it; the Prophet asked where, and affirmed the poet's answer, Paradise, God willing.
rows.anchor: وعن النابغه الجعدي أنه لما انشد رسول الله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Idris worships God with the angels in the seventh heaven and sometimes visits Paradise as he wishes.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة أنه عليه السلام يعبد الله تعالى مع الملائكة عليهم السلام في السماء السابعة ويرتع تاره في الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most who take the ascent physically say Idris remains alive in heaven; Muqatil's claim that he is dead there is anomalous.
rows.anchor: واكثر القائلين برفعة حسا قائلون بأنه حي حيث رفع وعن مقاتل أنه ميت في السماء وهو قول شاذ

rows.speaker: كعب وغيره
rows.claim: A report from Kaʿb and others says Idris asked God to ease the sun-bearer angel's heat and load; the grateful angel sought companionship and then helped Idris ascend. Al-Alusi leaves the report's authenticity uncertain.
rows.anchor: وسبب رفعه على ما روى عن كعب وغيره أنه مر ذات يوم في حاجة فاصابه وهج الشمس

rows.speaker: عمر مولى عفرة
rows.claim: A report raised to the Prophet says Idris was pious, divided his time between teaching, travel, and worship, befriended the Angel of Death, refused to take sheep or grapes without permission, and learned his companion's identity.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن عمر مولى عفره يرفع الحديث إلى النبى

rows.speaker: عمر مولى عفرة
rows.claim: In that account Idris asks to experience death and is restored, then visits Hell and Paradise; he cites the statements that every soul tastes death, everyone will come to Hell, and the people of Paradise will not be expelled, so God orders the Angel of Death to leave him there.
rows.anchor: فاحتضن بساق شجرة من اشجارها وقال : ما انا بخارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says this account and the preceding story from Kaʿb may or may not be authentic.
rows.anchor: والله تعالى أعلم بصحته وكذا بصحة ما قبله من خبر كعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ascension is praiseworthy when it signifies high rank and honor; mere physical elevation to a high place means little, since smoke and dust also rise.
rows.anchor: وهذا الرفع لاقتضائه علو الشأن ورفعة القدر كان فيه من المدح ما فيه وإلا فمجرد الرفع إلى مكان عالى حسا ليس بشئ

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some argue that “place” makes a physical elevation more likely; al-Alusi responds that scripture and poetry use comparable spatial language metaphorically too.
rows.anchor: وادعى بعضهم أن الأقرب أن العلو حسي لأن الرفعه المقترنة بالمكان لاتكون معنويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those” points to the people mentioned in the surah; its distance form signals their elevated rank and remote station of virtue.
rows.anchor: اشارة إلى المذكورين في السورة الكريمة وما فيه من معنى البعد للاشعار بعلو مرتبتهم وبعد منزلتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those whom God favored” refers to varied religious and worldly blessings; it is likely the predicate, while any restriction is relative to other people rather than the remaining prophets.
rows.anchor: أي بفنون النعم الدينية والدنيوية حسبما اشير اليه مجملا خبره على ما استظهره في البحر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some posit an omitted “some,” while another reading makes “among the prophets” partitive because those described are only some prophets receiving the blessings specified here.
rows.anchor: يقدر مضاف أي بعض الذين انعم الله عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From Adam's descendants” may explain the preceding phrase or be partitive; the partitive reading distinguishes those favored from the broader descendants while allowing overlap.
rows.anchor: قيل بيانيه والجار والمجرور بدل من الجار والمجرور السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those carried with Noah are descendants of his passengers other than Idris, who preceded Noah; Abraham was unanimously a descendant of Shem son of Noah.
rows.anchor: خصوصا وهم من عدا ادريس عليه السلام لما سمعت من أنه قبل نوح وابراهيم عليه السلام كان بالأجماع من ذرية سام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Israel” means Jacob; Moses, Aaron, Zechariah, John, and Jesus are among his descendants.
rows.anchor: أي ومن ذرية اسرائيل أي يعقوب عليه السلام وكان منهم موسى وهرون وزكريا ويحيى وعيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Including Jesus, who had no father, shows that descendants include a daughter's children; treating his inclusion as mere grammatical predominance is less apparent.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دليل على أن اولاد البنات من الذرية لدخول عيسى عليه السلام ولا اب له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Among those We guided and chose” coordinates with Adam's descendants and means some of those guided to truth and selected for prophethood and honor.
rows.anchor: ومن للتبعيض أي ومن جملة من هديناهم إلى الحق واخترناهم للنبوه والكرامة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative coordinates the phrase with “the prophets” and treats “from” as explanatory, but it must explain the apparent distinction between the groups.
rows.anchor: ومن للبيان واورد عليه أن ظاهر العطف المغايرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final clause begins a new sentence describing their awe and humility before God despite their lofty rank, noble lineage, and closeness to Him.
rows.anchor: استئناف مساق لبيان خشيته من الله تعالى واخباتهم له سبحانه مع ما لهم من علو الرتبة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Alternative syntaxes make the clause a second predicate or break the sentence after “Israel,” treating “among those We guided” as the predicate of an omitted subject; this latter analysis is attributed to Abu Muslim.
rows.anchor: خبر بعد خبر لاسم الأشارة

rows.speaker: علي بن الحسين
rows.claim: An Imami report from Ali ibn al-Husayn identifies the people as his family; al-Alusi calls this far from the apparent meaning and questions the reports' reliability.
rows.anchor: وروى بعض الأماميه عن علي بن الحسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi favors making the relative clause an adjective of the demonstrative and the final sentence its predicate, since that arrangement praises them most.
rows.anchor: وظاهر صنيع بعض المحققين اختيار أن يكون الموصول صفه لاسم الأشارة على ما هو الشائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Prostrating” is the plural of one who prostrates; “weeping” is the plural of one who weeps, with assimilation of the weak letters, though its expected regular plural is unattested according to al-Bahr.
rows.anchor: وسجدا جمع ساجد وكذا بكيا جمع باك كشاهد وشهود واصله بكوى اجتمعت الواو والياء

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: After reciting Maryam and prostrating, Umar remarked, “This is a prostration, but where is the weeping?”; the author rejects the claim that this forces a verbal-noun reading.
rows.anchor: عن عمر رضى الله تعالى عنه أنه قرأ سورة مريم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both accusatives describe the people as they fell, with prostration apparently the ritual act; the verses can be any revealed scripture, whether or not they mention prostration or punishment.
rows.anchor: أي ساجدين وباكين والأول حال مقدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense supports recommending prostration and weeping when reciting the Qur'an; a report from Saʿid ibn Abi Waqqas urges readers to weep, or feign weeping if unable.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا استدل بالآيه على استحباب السجود والبكى عند تلاوة القرآن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other interpretations make this the prostration of recitation at designated verses, prayer, or humble submission before verses about punishment; the prayer interpretation is strongly rejected.
rows.anchor: المراد من السجود سجود التلاوة حسب ما تعبدنا به

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi infers that prostration of recitation is obligatory; al-Kiya says that conclusion is far-fetched, as al-Alusi agrees.
rows.anchor: ونقل الجلال السيوطي عن الرازي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worshipper may make a fitting supplication at each recitation prostration, such as asking to be among the favored, guided, prostrating, and weeping servants here.
rows.anchor: وذكروا أنه ينبغي أن يدعو الساجد في سجدته بما يليق بايتها

rows.speaker: عبد الله وأبو جعفر وشيبة وشبل بن عباد وأبو حيوة وعبد الله بن أحمد العجلي عن حمزة وقتيبة وورش وابن ذكوان
rows.claim: These readers pronounce the verb with a masculine yāʾ, since the feminine subject is nonhuman and a phrase intervenes.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله وابو جعفر وشيبة وشبل ابن عباد وابو حيوة وعبد الله بن أحمد العجلي عن حمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual contrast is that khalaf with a still lām means bad successors, while khalaf with an open lām means their opposite, good successors.
rows.anchor: فان المشهورة في الخلف ساكن اللام ذلك والمشهور في مفتوح اللام ضده

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim says the form with sukūn means descendants, singular or plural, and the form with fatḥ means a replacement, whether a child or someone else.
rows.anchor: الخلف بالسكون الاولاد الجمع والواحد فيه سواء

rows.speaker: النضر بن شميل
rows.claim: Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl uses both vocalizations for a wicked generation and reserves the open-lām form for a righteous one.
rows.anchor: الخلف بالتحريك والاسكان القرن السوء

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jarir says praise most often uses the open lām and blame the still lām, though the pattern can reverse; Labid's verse uses the open form negatively.
rows.anchor: اكثر ما جاء في المدح بفتح اللام وفي الذم

rows.speaker: عبد الله والحسن وأبو رزين والضحاك وابن مقسم
rows.claim: These readers have the plural “prayers”; the singular can refer collectively because all prayers are one kind.
rows.anchor: بالجمع وهو ظاهر ولعل الأفراد للاتفاق في النوع

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود والنخعي والقاسم بن مخيمرة ومجاهد وإبراهيم وعمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: These authorities, and an Imami report from Abu Abd Allah, define neglecting prayer as delaying it beyond its appointed time.
rows.anchor: واضاعتها على ما روى عن ابن مسعود والنخعي والقاسم ابن مخيمرة ومجاهد وابراهيم وعمر بن عبد العزيز تاخيرها عن وقتها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says neglect means violating the prayer's conditions, including its time; other views say it means praying outside a congregation or abandoning prayer altogether.
rows.anchor: واختار الزجاج أن اضاعتها الاختلال بشروطها من الوقت وغيره

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi interprets neglect as abandoning prayer; another view makes it denial of prayer's obligation and thus applies the verse to unbelievers.
rows.anchor: أن اضاعتها تركها وقيل : عدم اعتقاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the verse means denial of obligation, it concerns unbelievers; other senses appear to concern Muslims, since unbelievers are not accountable for religious duties, unless this describes their characteristic conduct.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا الآية في الكفار وعلى ما قبله لاقطعواستظر انها عليه في قوم مسلمين بناء على أن الكفار غير مكلفين بالفروع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Muqatil identify the people as Jews; al-Suddi includes Jews and Christians. Al-Alusi prefers unbelievers generally, while Mujahid, Qatada, and Ata identify Muslims in this community who later practice public, shameless sex.
rows.anchor: والمشهور عن ابن عباس ومقاتل انها في اليهودوعن السدى انها فيهم وفي النصارى واختير كونها في الكفرة مطلقا

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Bahr says “desires” covers anything that distracts from prayer and remembrance of God; an example about marrying a paternal half-sister is not sound, while Ali described people who build ostentatiously, ride fine mounts, and wear famous clothing.
rows.anchor: عام في كل مشتهى يشغل عن الصلاة وعن ذكر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو أمامة
rows.claim: A report from Abu Umama attributed to the Prophet describes ghayy as a river at the bottom of Hell carrying the inhabitants' pus; a stone cast from its brink takes seventy years to reach its bottom, past Ghayy and Atham.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن جرير والطبراني وغيرهما من حديث أبى امامة مرفوعا أنه نهر في اسفل جهنم يسيل فيه صديد أهل النار

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿud calls ghayy a deep, foul river or valley of Hell into which those who follow desires are cast.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود أنه قال : الغى نهر أو واد

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani describes ghayy as a pit in Hell into which pus and exudate flow.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكرمانى أنه ابار في جهنم يسيل اليها الصديد والقيح

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada takes ghayy to mean evil or misery, illustrating the usage with a verse by al-Muraqqish al-Asghar about the blame that follows someone who goes astray.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبى حاتم عن قتادة أن الغى السوء ومن ذلك قول مرقش الأصغر

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والضحاك والزجاج
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd gives the common meaning “misguidance”; al-Dahhak says it is the requital for misguidance, and al-Zajjaj prefers that interpretation. Another view means straying from the path to Paradise.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن زيد أنه الضلال وهو المعنى المشهور وعليه قيل المراد جزاء غى وروى ذلك عن الضحاك واخياره الزجاج

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reports a passive reading of the verb, with a doubled qaf.
rows.anchor: بضم اليء وفتح اللام وشد القاف

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj treats the exception as disconnected; al-Bahr says its apparent form is connected, and the mention of faith suggests an audience of unbelievers or a general audience addressed emphatically.
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع عند الزجاج وقال في البحر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Faith may mean prayer, as in “your faith,” so it answers neglecting prayer, while righteous deeds answer following desires.
rows.anchor: المراد من الأيمان الصلاة كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised entrants are those with repentance, faith, and righteous action; their entry is assured without delay, and nothing is withheld from their reward.
rows.anchor: المنعوتون بالتوبة والأيمان والعمل الصالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They will not be wronged” means their reward is not diminished; it also indicates their earlier sins will neither harm them nor reduce their reward.
rows.anchor: من جزاء اعمالهم شيئا أو لاينقصون

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وأبو بكر ويعقوب
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Abu Bakr, and Yaqub read “they enter” in the active voice; Ibn Ghazwan from Talha reads “they will enter” with the future marker.
rows.anchor: وقرا ابن كثير وابو عمرو وابو بكر ويعقوب

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila infer that good deeds are a condition for entering Paradise; al-Alusi answers that the contrast concerns entering without delay, not entry into Paradise in every sense.
rows.anchor: واستدل المعتزلة بالآية على أن العمل شرط دخول الجنة وأجيب بأن المراد يدخلون الجنة بلا تسويف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other replies make deeds a condition for entering the Garden of Eden in particular or for receiving full reward; al-Alusi finds the latter reply unconvincing.
rows.anchor: وايضا يجوز أن يكون شرطا لدخول جنة عدن لامطلق الجنة وقيل هو شرط لعدم نقص شيئ من ثواب الأعمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An objection says the condition would exclude a repentant believer who dies before managing a good deed; the answer is that rulings rest on the general case, not rare exceptions.
rows.anchor: من تاب وآمن ولم يتمكن من العمل الصالح يدخل الجنه وأجيب بأن ذلك من الصور النادرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Gardens of Eden” apposes “Paradise” as a part contained within the whole, if Eden is the proper name of one of the eight gardens.
rows.anchor: بدل من الجنة بدل البعض لاشتمالها عليها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view makes Garden of Eden a proper name for one of eight gardens; another treats the whole phrase as a proper name formed by retaining the second element after dropping the first.
rows.anchor: علم لاحدى الجنات الثمان كعلمية بنات اوبر

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Al-Kashf says that in a proper name formed from a genitive phrase, Arabic treats the genitive element as the proper name, as with kunyas; forms such as Bint Awbar and Ibn Daya support this usage.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف اذا كانت التسمية بالمضاف والمضاف اليه جعلوا المضاف اليه في نحوه مقدر العلمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Eden can derive as a noun of remaining in a place; the phrase is definite on either proper-name account, while making the first element generic and the second proper requires a strained generic-to-specific construction.
rows.anchor: وإن لم يكن عدن في الأصل علما ولا معرفة بل هو مصدر عدن بالمكان يعدن ويعدن أقام به

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan allows “gardens of residence and stability” as an indefinite phrase, rejects requiring the proper-name claim without Arabic evidence, and says grammar permits an indefinite appositive without an adjective; praise accusative is also possible.
rows.anchor: وجوز أبو حيان اعتبار جنات عدن نكرة على معنى جنات إقامة واستقرار

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali allows an indefinite appositive when it adds information absent from its antecedent; the relative clause may also be an appositive rather than an adjective.
rows.anchor: يجوز ذلك إذا كان في إبدال النكرة فائدة لا تستفاد
